title: Industry applications of neutral-atom quantum computing solving independent set problems
abstract_summary: This preprint reviews how neutral-atom (Rydberg) quantum computers naturally encode independent set problems via the Rydberg blockade and surveys industry-relevant applications across telecommunications, logistics, finance, drug discovery and network design. It describes embeddings and algorithms (adiabatic, variational, sampling and quantum machine learning) for solving or sampling independent-set-based combinatorial optimizations and provides concrete example mappings and use cases demonstrating how current and near-term neutral-atom devices can address these problems.
methodology_description: This preprint is a conceptual and methodological exposition showing how independent-set combinatorial optimization problems can be encoded natively in neutral-atom (Rydberg) quantum processors and how those encodings can be used (directly or via reductions) for industry-relevant tasks including finance. The core mapping uses the Rydberg Hamiltonian in analog mode: single-atom drives (Rabi frequencies Omega_j, phases phi_j) and detunings Delta_j control transitions between a ground |1> and a Rydberg |r> state, while pairwise van der Waals interactions C6/|r_j - r_k|^6 produce a blockade such that the low-energy subspace corresponds to independent sets of a unit-disk graph whose radius R_b = (C6/Delta)^(1/6). Two embedding strategies are described: a native embedding where atom positions map directly to unit-disk graph vertices, and a hybrid (gadgetization) embedding that maps arbitrary graphs to unit-disk graphs at polynomial ancilla overhead (O(N) for many 2D-geometric graphs, up to O(N^2) in general). Algorithmic approaches described include adiabatic state preparation (slowly evolving to the classical ground state which encodes MWIS), variational algorithms (QAOA-style and general variational ansatz), variational quantum sampling / generative modeling to produce biased distributions over independent sets, and quantum-classical hybrid workflows where quantum-sampled independent sets are classically post-processed (e.g., to produce dominating or connected dominating sets). The paper also details reductions from other combinatorial problems (graph coloring, SAT, QUBO, etc.) into MIS encodings suitable for Rydberg arrays, and suggests hybrid QML training loops to fit problem-specific probability weights (e.g., Boltzmann-like weights) when optimization objectives go beyond simple Hamiltonian energies.

key_findings: [supported] Neutral-atom (Rydberg) quantum processors provide a natural, hardware-native encoding of independent set constraints via the Rydberg blockade mechanism (mapping atoms in Rydberg state to vertices in an independent set).
[supported] QuEra’s Aquila device is a 256-qubit neutral-atom quantum computer (product/existence claim).

[supported] An experimental demonstration (Ebadi et al., Science 2022) showed Rydberg atom arrays solving MIS instances and reported a superlinear quantum speedup compared to a class of generic classical algorithms.

[speculative] The classical ground state (Ω = 0, Δ > 0) of the Rydberg Hamiltonian encodes the maximum weight independent set of the corresponding unit disk graph (theoretical mapping / algorithmic proposal).

[speculative] Adiabatic, QAOA-style, variational, and quantum machine-learning approaches on Rydberg platforms can be used to prepare low-energy/biased sampling states to find or sample independent sets (algorithmic proposals).

[speculative] Sampling from quantum-prepared wavefunctions over independent sets can be leveraged for #P-hard statistical tasks (e.g., partition functions, expectation values) that are hard to simulate classically.

[speculative] Many industry problems (antenna placement, portfolio construction, molecular docking, network immunization, 5G gateway design, ad-hoc routing, telecommunication loss networks, incremental store placement, task scheduling) can be mapped to independent set (or related) problems and thus potentially target neutral-atom hardware.

[speculative] Unit disk graphs (UDGs) can be embedded natively on 2D neutral-atom arrays with no overhead, while general graphs can be embedded into unit disk graphs using ancilla atoms at polynomial overhead (claims: O(N) ancilla for graphs with underlying 2D structure; O(N^2) atoms for arbitrary general graphs).

[speculative] Quantum-assisted hybrid schemes (sampling from quantum device + classical post-processing) are promising for problems that are not directly ground-state encodable (e.g., dominating sets, connected dominating sets).
[speculative] Variationally prepared quantum distributions could be trained (QML) to match desired weighted ensemble statistics of maximal independent sets for decision-making under uncertainty.
[speculative] Reductions from other NP problems (graph coloring, SAT, QUBO, paint shop) to MIS enable a broader set of combinatorial problems to be targeted by Rydberg-based devices.
[speculative] The Rydberg blockade radius can be tuned via detuning and interaction parameters (Rb = (C6/Δ)^(1/6)) enabling control of the encoded unit disk radius in practice.

[speculative] Neutral-atom quantum sampling machines could serve as practical variational samplers for distributions that are classically hard to reproduce (#P-hard), enabling new probabilistic/ML workflows.

[speculative] Practical near-term advantage will depend on careful problem-to-hardware matchmaking and hybrid quantum-classical pipelines rather than pure end-to-end quantum supremacy for broad problem classes.
results_summary: The preprint reviews how neutral-atom, Rydberg-based quantum processors naturally encode independent set constraints through the Rydberg blockade and outlines algorithmic paradigms (adiabatic, variational/QAOA, sampling, and quantum machine learning) to find or sample independent sets and related combinatorial problems. It catalogs many industry-relevant problem mappings (antenna placement, portfolio selection via clique complements, molecular docking, network immunization, 5G gateway placement, ad-hoc routing, telecommunication loss networks, incremental store planning, scheduling via coloring, etc.) and discusses embedding strategies (native unit-disk embedding and gadget-based hybrid embeddings with ancilla overhead). The paper emphasizes hybrid quantum-classical workflows for problems not directly encoded in ground states and cites an experimental demonstration (Science 2022) reporting a superlinear speedup on MIS instances using Rydberg arrays. Overall, the work positions neutral-atom platforms as a promising, hardware-native approach for a broad class of combinatorial optimization and sampling tasks, while acknowledging practical embedding and algorithmic challenges.
performance_claims: Aquila: 256-qubit neutral-atom quantum computer (QuEra product claim).

Experimental demonstration (Ebadi et al., Science 2022) reporting a superlinear quantum speedup for MIS relative to a class of generic classical algorithms (no single-number scaling in this preprint).
Rydberg interaction scaling ∝ 1/R^6 and blockade radius formula Rb = (C6/Δ)^(1/6) (physical-parameter relation).

Embedding overhead claims: geometric (2D) graphs can be encoded with O(N) ancilla atoms; arbitrary general graphs can be embedded into unit disk graphs with at most O(N^2) atoms (reduction/embedding complexity claims).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper cites (and builds on) an experimental result (Ebadi et al., Science 2022) that reported a superlinear speedup of Rydberg-atom arrays solving MIS instances versus a class of generic classical algorithms. This constitutes an empirical demonstration on specific problem families and instance sizes; however, the work and the preprint are careful to present this as a promising instance-class advantage rather than a proven broad, asymptotic quantum advantage for all combinatorial optimization problems.
limitations: Noisy hardware and limited qubit counts on near-term devices restrict applicability to only certain problem sizes and types (author-stated).

The neutral-atom analog-mode Rydberg encoding naturally maps unit disk graphs (UDGs); non-geometric/general graphs require gadgetization or hybrid embeddings with extra atoms and overhead (author-stated).

Mapping arbitrary general graphs to unit-disk embeddings can require polynomial overhead in atom count (stated upper bound O(N^2), and O(N) for graphs with underlying 2D geometry) which may be prohibitive in practice (author-stated).

Many independent-set related problems remain NP-hard/#P-hard (MIS NP-hard, counting independent sets #P-complete, MIS approximability hardness etc.), so exact solutions are intractable classically and also pose limits on what near-term quantum devices can guarantee (author-stated).

Problems such as minimum dominating set (MDS) and minimum connected dominating set (MCDS) are not directly encoded as ground states of the Rydberg Hamiltonian and therefore require hybrid variational/sampling + classical post-processing approaches (author-stated).
Analog-mode operation of current neutral-atom devices is less general than a full digital universal model; the digital/multi-qubit gate mode is presented as future work (author-stated).

The reported experimental algorithmic improvements (e.g., superlinear speedup) are demonstrated against particular classes of classical algorithms/benchmarks, not proven to generalize to all classical heuristics or all instance families (author-stated/inferred).

[inferred] Gadgetization and hybrid embedding overheads (extra atoms, larger arrays, more control complexity) may make many practical problem instances infeasible on current or near-term neutral-atom devices.

[inferred] Adiabatic ground-state preparation and quantum annealing approaches can be limited by small spectral gaps and long required evolution times (run-time/resource scaling concern), which is not addressed in detail.

[inferred] Variational and sampling approaches rely on classical optimization of parameters (and on ansatz expressiveness); they are vulnerable to classical bottlenecks such as noisy gradients, barren plateaus, or local minima, which may limit performance.

[inferred] Classical post-processing steps required for translating sampled independent sets into solutions for non-native problems (e.g., making sampled sets dominating/connected) may incur significant computational cost that could negate some quantum advantages.

[inferred] Precision and stability requirements on atom placement, control of Rydberg interactions, and calibration (e.g., for setting blockade radius accurately) imply engineering limitations that may affect real-world problem encodings.

[inferred] The paper mostly outlines potential application mappings and algorithm classes (adiabatic, QAOA, QML, sampling) but lacks comprehensive empirical resource estimates (atoms, time, fidelity) for industrial-scale instances, leaving practical feasibility unclear.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Rydberg blockade provides a native hardware encoding of Maximum Independent Set (MIS), enabling direct mappings of many industry problems (including portfolio selection via clique complements) to neutral-atom devices and citing Ebadi et al. (2022) as an experimental demonstration with reported superlinear speedup for MIS.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Native unit-disk graph embeddings on 2D neutral-atom arrays and existing devices (e.g., QuEra Aquila, ~256 qubits) suggest some small-to-moderate problem instances and sampling tasks could be accessible in the near term with careful problem-hardware matching.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Advocates hybrid workflows where quantum-prepared samples (independent sets) are classically post-processed to produce solutions for problems not directly encoded (e.g., dominating/connected dominating sets), and where classical optimizers train variational/QML circuits.

#limitation:qubit-count — Embedding arbitrary graphs into unit-disk Rydberg encodings can require polynomial ancilla overhead (claims up to O(N^2) atoms in worst case), implying many practical problems will exceed current device capacities.

#limitation:data-encoding — Gadgetization/reductions from general graphs or QUBO to unit-disk graphs introduce encoding overhead and complexity, raising costs for realistic financial problem instances.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — This work is a conceptual/methodological survey; most claims and industry mappings are speculative and not accompanied by new empirical benchmarks or experiments in this paper.

#limitation:noise — Recommended adiabatic/variational approaches and sampling-based workflows are NISQ-era methods that will be sensitive to noise and coherence times; practical performance depends on error rates and mitigation not addressed empirically here.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Suggests variational quantum sampling on Rydberg arrays could target classically hard (#P-hard) distributions for probabilistic/ML workflows, but this remains a speculative research direction requiring further validation.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Emphasizes that practical benefit is likely to come from hybrid, problem-specific pipelines and careful embeddings rather than broad end-to-end quantum supremacy across finance tasks.
